meta.titre: Animal Hormones: How Chemical Messengers Coordinate the Body
meta.sous_theme: Nature, action and examples of hormones

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader in Mile 17 market runs to catch the last bus to Buea. Within seconds her heart is pounding and her breathing is fast, long before she has had time to think about it. A hormone, adrenaline, has been released into her blood and is already at work. Hormones control growth, water balance, blood sugar, reproduction and stress responses, so the GCE Advanced Level paper keeps asking what hormones are, how they travel and why only some cells respond. This lesson gives you the exact words and examples that examiners reward.

items: Blood plasma transports dissolved substances around the body.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids and steroids are lipids built on a four-ring carbon skeleton.
Homeostasis keeps the internal environment of the body within narrow limits.
A receptor is a molecule with a specific shape to which only a complementary molecule can bind.

sections.titre: Hormones: definition, characteristics, chemical types and mode of action
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **hormone** is a chemical messenger produced by an **endocrine gland** (a ductless gland) or by specialised cells, secreted directly into the blood and carried to **target cells** that have specific receptors for it. The hormone changes the activity of those cells.

**Characteristics of hormones**
- They are made in one tissue and act on a different tissue; they are not made in the cells that they affect.
- They are transported in the blood plasma, so they reach every part of the body, but only target cells with the right receptor respond.
- They are effective in very small quantities, and a small amount can produce a large effect.
- They are specific: the shape of the hormone is complementary to the shape of its receptor.
- Their effects are usually slower to start and longer lasting than the effect of a nerve impulse.
- They are broken down, mostly in the liver, and the products are excreted by the kidneys, so the effect does not go on for ever.
- Several hormones may work together or oppose one another (insulin and glucagon are antagonistic).

**Chemical types and where the receptor is**

| Type | Examples | Where the receptor is | Mode of action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peptides and proteins (water-soluble) | insulin, glucagon, ADH, oxytocin, FSH, LH | On the cell surface membrane | Cannot cross the membrane; binding triggers a second messenger (cyclic AMP) inside the cell, which activates enzymes |
| Amino acid derivatives | adrenaline; thyroxine | Adrenaline: cell surface. Thyroxine: inside the cell | Adrenaline uses a second messenger; thyroxine enters the cell and affects gene expression |
| Steroids (lipid-soluble) | oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone, cortisol, aldosterone | Inside the cell (cytoplasm or nucleus) | Pass through the phospholipid bilayer; the hormone-receptor complex switches particular genes on or off |

**Control by negative feedback.** The level of most hormones is kept steady because a rise in the effect of the hormone is detected and the secretion of the hormone is reduced; a fall has the opposite result.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on antagonistic hormones, diabetes or the pancreas.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
The **islets of Langerhans** in the pancreas contain **beta cells**, which secrete **insulin** when blood glucose is high, and **alpha cells**, which secrete **glucagon** when it is low.

- **Insulin** makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose, converts glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis) and increases the use of glucose in respiration. Blood glucose falls.
- **Glucagon** makes liver cells break glycogen down to glucose (glycogenolysis) and form glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (gluconeogenesis). Blood glucose rises.

Each hormone corrects a change in the opposite direction, so the blood glucose concentration swings around a set point: this is negative feedback.

variantes.nom: Water balance and blood pressure: ADH and renin
variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on kidneys, dehydration or low blood pressure.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**ADH (antidiuretic hormone)** is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus and released from the **posterior pituitary**. When the blood becomes too concentrated, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect it, more ADH is released, the collecting ducts become more permeable to water and more water is reabsorbed. A small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

**Renin** is an enzyme released by kidney cells when blood pressure or blood volume falls. It converts the plasma protein angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release **aldosterone**. Aldosterone makes the kidney reabsorb sodium ions, water follows, and blood volume and pressure rise.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on stress, the adrenal glands or a rapid hormonal response.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Adrenaline** is secreted by the **adrenal medulla** when the brain senses danger or excitement. It increases heart rate and breathing rate, stimulates the breakdown of glycogen so blood glucose rises, widens the bronchioles, dilates the pupils, and redirects blood from the skin and gut to the skeletal muscles. The body is prepared for vigorous activity.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Two adults, one healthy and one with untreated diabetes mellitus (lack of insulin action), each drink a glucose solution at time 0. Their blood glucose concentrations are recorded in mg per 100 cm³ of blood.

| Time / min | 0 | 30 | 60 | 120 | 180 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Healthy person | 90 | 140 | 110 | 95 | 90 |
| Person with diabetes | 180 | 290 | 320 | 310 | 290 |

(a) Calculate the percentage rise in the healthy person's blood glucose during the first 30 minutes. (b) Calculate the mean rate at which the healthy person's blood glucose fell between 30 and 120 minutes. (c) Compare this with the rate at which the glucose of the person with diabetes fell from its highest value to 180 minutes. (d) Explain the difference in terms of hormones.

etapes.action: Percentage rise in the healthy person (0 to 30 min)
Rate of fall in the healthy person (30 to 120 min)
etapes.justification: Rate = change in concentration / time taken, with units.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Fall = 140 − 95 = 45 mg per 100 cm³ in 90 min; 45 / 90 = **0.5 mg per 100 cm³ per min**.

etapes.action: Rate of fall for the person with diabetes
etapes.justification: The highest value is 320 mg per 100 cm³ at 60 min, so the fall is measured from 60 to 180 min.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Fall = 320 − 290 = 30 in 120 min; 30 / 120 = **0.25 mg per 100 cm³ per min**, half the healthy rate.

etapes.action: Compare the shape of the two curves
etapes.justification: Both rise after absorption, but only one returns to the starting value.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The healthy person is back to 90 by 180 min; the person with diabetes is still 290, about 3.2 times the healthy value (290 / 90), and began from a higher fasting value.

etapes.justification: Name the gland, the cells, the hormone and its effect on target cells.
etapes.resultat_markdown: High glucose stimulates beta cells of the islets of Langerhans to secrete insulin. Insulin makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, so blood glucose falls. In diabetes insulin is lacking (or target cells do not respond), so glucose uptake is slow and the concentration stays high.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Insulin is the hormone that lowers blood glucose; without its action the glucose level rises higher, stays high for longer and falls at about half the normal rate.

items.erreur_markdown: Hormones are carried from the gland to the target organ along ducts.
items.pourquoi_faux: Endocrine glands are ductless. Ducts belong to exocrine glands, such as salivary glands.
items.correction_markdown: Hormones are secreted directly into the blood capillaries and carried by the blood plasma to the whole body.

items.erreur_markdown: A hormone acts on every cell that it reaches.
items.pourquoi_faux: The hormone reaches all cells, but only cells with a receptor of complementary shape respond.
items.correction_markdown: Say that **only target cells with specific receptors** respond to a given hormone.

items.erreur_markdown: Insulin raises blood glucose and glucagon lowers it.
items.pourquoi_faux: The roles are reversed. Insulin is secreted when glucose is high and lowers it; glucagon is secreted when glucose is low and raises it.
items.correction_markdown: Insulin: glucose to glycogen, glucose falls. Glucagon: glycogen to glucose, glucose rises.

items.erreur_markdown: ADH is made in the posterior pituitary gland.
items.pourquoi_faux: ADH is made in neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus. The posterior pituitary stores it and releases it into the blood.
items.correction_markdown: ADH is **made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary**.

items.erreur_markdown: Hormonal control is as fast and short-lived as nervous control.
items.pourquoi_faux: Hormones travel in the blood and usually act more slowly, and their effects last longer than those of nerve impulses.
items.correction_markdown: Nervous: fast, short-lived, localised. Hormonal: slower, longer lasting, widespread.

items.enonce_markdown: Classify each of these hormones as a peptide/protein, an amino acid derivative or a steroid, and say whether its receptor is on the cell surface or inside the cell: (i) cortisol, (ii) glucagon, (iii) adrenaline, (iv) testosterone.
items.solution_markdown: (i) Cortisol: **steroid; receptor inside the cell**. (ii) Glucagon: **peptide/protein; receptor on the cell surface**. (iii) Adrenaline: **amino acid derivative; receptor on the cell surface**. (iv) Testosterone: **steroid; receptor inside the cell**. Steroids are lipid-soluble and pass through the phospholipid bilayer; peptides cannot, so they bind to surface receptors and use a second messenger.

items.enonce_markdown: A student drinks 1.0 dm³ of water at time 0 and the volume of urine produced is measured every 15 minutes. Before the drink the volume was 8 cm³ per 15 minutes. After the drink the volumes in successive 15-minute periods were 10, 35, 60, 55, 25 and 9 cm³. (a) Calculate the total volume of urine produced in the 90 minutes after the drink and express it as a percentage of the water drunk. (b) Calculate the highest rate of urine production in cm³ per min and how many times it exceeds the rate before the drink. (c) Explain the change using ADH.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Total = 10 + 35 + 60 + 55 + 25 + 9 = 194 cm³; 194 / 1000 × 100 = **19.4 %**.

(b) Highest volume 60 cm³ in 15 min = 60 / 15 = **4.0 cm³ per min**. Before the drink: 8 cm³ per 15 min, so 60 / 8 = **7.5 times** the earlier rate.

(c) The extra water dilutes the blood, which raises its water potential. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this, less ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, the collecting ducts become less permeable to water, less water is reabsorbed and a large volume of dilute urine is produced. As the blood returns to normal, ADH secretion rises and the urine volume falls back.

items.enonce_markdown: In an experiment on anaesthetised dogs, acid was placed in the duodenum and the volume of pancreatic juice secreted in 10 minutes was collected. Results: nerves to the duodenum intact, 12.0 cm³; all nerves to the duodenum cut, 11.5 cm³; an extract of the lining of the duodenum treated with acid and injected into a vein, 11.8 cm³; acid injected into a vein, 0.3 cm³; an extract of muscle treated with acid and injected into a vein, 0.4 cm³. (a) Calculate the secretion with the nerves cut as a percentage of the secretion with the nerves intact. (b) What do the results show about the control of the pancreas? (c) Why were the last two treatments included? (d) Name the hormone and the target organ.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 11.5 / 12.0 × 100 = **95.8 %**.

(b) Secretion is almost unchanged when the nerves are cut, and the extract of the duodenal lining produces nearly the same response when it is carried in the blood (11.8 cm³, 98.3 % of the intact value). So the signal from the duodenum to the pancreas is **chemical and travels in the blood**, not along nerves. The duodenal lining releases a hormone when acid arrives.

(c) They are **controls**: acid alone injected into the blood, and an extract of another tissue, give almost no secretion (0.3 and 0.4 cm³). This shows that the response is not caused by the acid itself or by any tissue extract, only by the duodenal lining extract.

(d) The hormone is **secretin**; the target organ is the **pancreas**, which responds with a watery, alkaline secretion that neutralises the acid.

items_markdown: A hormone is a chemical messenger made by an endocrine (ductless) gland, secreted into the blood and acting on target cells with specific receptors.
Hormones act in small quantities, are specific, are slower and longer lasting than nerve impulses, and are broken down in the liver.
Peptide hormones bind to surface receptors and use a second messenger; steroid hormones enter the cell and affect genes.
Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it: antagonistic hormones in negative feedback.
ADH, made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary, increases water reabsorption; renin starts the pathway that releases aldosterone.
Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight within seconds.
